# Judges Chapter 20 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-09

---

### v.5 — "they violated my concubine" vs. "they raped my concubine"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "my concubine they humbled" | innah — standard OT verb for sexual violence |
| LOGOS | "they violated my concubine" | Formal, preserves the legal register |
| PNEUMA | "They raped my concubine" | Modern, unambiguous |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew innah (עָנָּה) is a legal term used throughout the Torah for sexual violence (cf. Deut 22:24, 29; 2 Sam 13:12, 14 — Tamar). It carries juridical weight that English "rape" conveys in modern usage but "violated" preserves in a literary register that matches the Levite's testimony before the assembly. PNEUMA's "raped" is not wrong — it is exactly what happened — but the formal legal context favors the formal term.

**Status:** Moderate. Register choice in a legal assembly context.

---

### v.13 — "worthless fellows" vs. "sons of Belial" vs. "wicked men"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "sons of B'liyya'al" | Transliteration of Hebrew |
| LOGOS | "worthless fellows" | Standard interpretive rendering |
| PNEUMA | "worthless men" | Same sense, slightly different |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. B'nei b'liyya'al is a compound phrase meaning "sons of worthlessness/destruction" — used for the men of Gibeah (19:22), the sons of Eli (1 Sam 2:12), and Nabal (1 Sam 25:17). "Worthless fellows" preserves the contempt without transliterating. EMET's transliteration is opaque; PNEUMA's "worthless men" is functionally identical to LOGOS.

**Status:** Minor. Standard religious vocabulary.

---

### v.18 — "Who shall go up first?" — Echo of 1:1

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "Who shall go up first for us to battle against the sons of Binyamin?" | Literal, preserves "sons of" |
| LOGOS | "Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?" | Formal, same structure as 1:1 |
| PNEUMA | "Which tribe should lead the attack against Benjamin?" | Dynamic, loses the verbal echo |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The phrase mi ya'aleh lanu bat'chilah ("who shall go up for us first?") is identical to 1:1. This is one of the most important literary inclusions in the book — the same question opens the conquest and opens the civil war. PNEUMA's "Which tribe should lead the attack?" loses the verbal parallel entirely. The echo must be preserved.

**Status:** Major. Literary inclusion — the book's structural bookend.

---

### v.34 — "the evil was touching them" vs. "disaster was close upon them" vs. "disaster was about to strike"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "the evil was touching them" | noge'a — literally "touching" |
| LOGOS | "disaster was close upon them" | Interprets naga' as proximity |
| PNEUMA | "disaster was about to strike" | Dynamic, temporal |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew noge'a (נֹגַ֥עַת) from naga' literally means "touching" — the evil/disaster was already in contact with them, they just didn't know it. "Close upon them" captures the imminence better than PNEUMA's "about to strike" (which implies it hasn't yet arrived). EMET's "touching" is technically accurate but sounds odd in English.

**Status:** Minor. Lexical nuance.

---

### v.48 — cherem language: "men and beasts" vs. "everyone — people, animals, everything"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "from the city, men to beast to all that was found" | Preserves m'tom ad-b'hemah |
| LOGOS | "the city, men and beasts and all that was found" | Formal, preserves structure |
| PNEUMA | "putting everyone to the sword — people, animals, everything they found" | Dynamic, adds "putting to sword" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The key phrase is m'ir m'tom ad-b'hemah — "from the city, from men to beast" — which echoes the cherem (holy-war destruction) formula applied to Canaanite cities. The precise wording matters: Israel applies to its own brother tribe the same destruction it was commanded to apply to Canaan. PNEUMA's expansion, while clear, adds "putting to the sword" which dilutes the formula's echo of Deuteronomy 13:15 and Joshua 6:21.

**Status:** Moderate. Cherem vocabulary — connects civil war to holy war.

---

## Summary of Disagreement Patterns

| Pattern | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Literary echo / inclusion | 1 | "Who shall go up first?" (v.18 / 1:1) — book's structural bookend |
| Register in formal context | 1 | innah rendering in assembly testimony (v.5) |
| Cherem vocabulary | 1 | Holy-war language applied to brother tribe (v.48) |
| Standard vocabulary | 1 | B'nei b'liyya'al rendering (v.13) |
| Lexical nuance | 1 | naga' — "touching" vs. "close upon" (v.34) |

**Overall pattern:** The critical disagreement is v.18 — the echo of 1:1. The question "Who shall go up first?" is the book's structural bookend, framing the entire narrative from conquest of Canaan to civil war against Benjamin. PNEUMA's dynamic rendering destroys this literary architecture.

---

*— SOPHIA, AI Translator, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
